analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal contracts and bans contractors for ten years after repeated wage-law violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees and its subcommittees until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires federal construction contractors to pay workers the local prevailing wage. This bill would have let the Labor Secretary cancel a federal contract and bar the contractor from new federal work for ten years after a pattern of wage violations, unless the contractor proved the violations were honest mistakes. It would also have opened contractors' payroll records, including employee names and addresses, to public inspection for audits.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would get a stronger remedy when contractors shortchange the required prevailing wages, and honest contractors who now compete against firms that cut labor costs by breaking wage rules.

how_it_helps.text: A contractor found to have a pattern of Davis-Bacon violations would lose its federal contract and be barred from federal contracts for ten years, a much sharper penalty than current enforcement provides.
The Labor Secretary could not impose the ban if the contractor showed the violations were unintentional and the result of simple, unsystematic errors, limiting the penalty to willful violators.
Payroll records from Davis-Bacon contracts, including employee names and addresses, would be open to inspection for audits even over privacy-law objections, making it easier to detect underpayment.

analysis.who_pays: Federal construction contractors who violate prevailing wage rules, who would face contract cancellation and a ten-year ban on federal work, plus the administrative cost of keeping payroll records open to auditors.

drawbacks.text: A mandatory ten-year ban is severe even for serious repeat violations, and opponents of Davis-Bacon enforcement argue such penalties shrink the pool of bidders and can raise federal construction costs.
Requiring disclosure of employee names and addresses under the Freedom of Information Act raises privacy concerns for workers whose payroll data would become inspectable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers on federal construction jobs, stronger penalties for wage cheating and auditable payroll records would directly protect the wages the law already promises them. The main costs fall on violators and on federal contracting through a smaller, costlier contractor pool; the privacy tradeoff on payroll disclosure is real but modest. A well-designed enforcement strengthening overall.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, sent down to their subcommittees, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on July 31, 2001, with no cosponsors.

It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Government Reform Committee, which split it between the Subcommittee on Technology and Procurement Policy and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
No further action was taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors who skirt prevailing wage rules are better off, since the threat of contract cancellation, a ten-year federal contract ban, and open payroll audits never materialized.

for.name: Rep. Robert Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Enforcement Act of 2001 to stiffen penalties for wage violations on federal contracts.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no action was taken.

against.name: House Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for its provisions on payroll disclosure and referred it to the Subcommittee on Technology and Procurement Policy, where no action was taken.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with zero cosponsors of either party and died in committee without any recorded votes, so no clear party split ever formed.

industries.note: Repeat violators of prevailing wage rules would lose their federal contracts and be barred from federal work for ten years, and all Davis-Bacon contractors' payroll records would be open to audit inspection. Their savings from underpaying workers come directly out of construction workers' pay.

Construction workers on federal projects would get a much stronger enforcement backstop for the prevailing wages the Davis-Bacon Act already guarantees them, since contractors who repeatedly underpay would face losing federal work entirely.
